title: Pre-Trained Vision-Language Model Selection and Reuse for Downstream Tasks

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to motivate the problem of selecting a pre-trained Vision-Language Model (VLM) per downstream task by showing that no single VLM dominates across tasks or even across classes within a task. Paper [5] explicitly addresses the challenge of selecting the best-performing VLM for downstream applications, noting that performance is dataset- and task-dependent. Paper [4] also discusses nuanced relationships between models and tasks in the context of model selection for downstream fine-tuning. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective of improving model selection for downstream tasks, making the purpose covered.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves empirical measurement of many open-clip VLMs across several downstream tasks and classes within a task, comparing per-task and per-class strengths. Paper [10] introduces VL-CheckList, a toolbox for fine-grained evaluation of VLMs, which includes analyzing the pros and cons of different VLMs across tasks. Paper [5] also discusses exhaustive evaluation of VLMs across downstream applications, which aligns with the empirical measurement mechanism. Both papers use substantively equivalent mechanisms for evaluating VLMs across tasks and classes, making the mechanism covered.

### Evaluation
The contribution's evaluation design is qualitative, showing distinct strengths of each VLM and that models weak on general tasks can surpass stronger ones on specific downstream tasks/classes. Paper [10] uses VL-CheckList for fine-grained evaluation of VLMs, which includes qualitative analysis of model strengths and weaknesses across tasks. Paper [5] also evaluates VLMs across downstream applications, focusing on their task-dependent performance. Both papers employ substantively equivalent evaluation designs, making the evaluation covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and model selection for visual classification. Paper [5] explicitly addresses the domain of pre-trained VLMs for downstream vision applications, including classification tasks. Paper [10] also focuses on evaluating VLMs for vision-language tasks, which includes visual classification. Both papers work in the same general application area, making the domain covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable scalable, data- and compute-efficient selection and reuse of vision-language models (VLMs) without evaluating every candidate on the target task. Paper [4] explicitly addresses the same problem: "selecting the best-performing VLM for some downstream applications is non-trivial, as it is dataset and task-dependent. Meanwhile, the exhaustive evaluation of all available VLMs on a novel application is not only time and computationally demanding." This matches the purpose at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces the Model Label Learning (MLL) paradigm, which includes three modules: model labeling (assigning task-independent labels via a semantic graph of visual concepts), model selection (matching target classes to semantic graph nodes via captions), and model reuse (top-k ensemble predictions). Paper [4] uses a language-only approach for VLM selection, but it does not employ a semantic graph or task-independent labeling. Paper [19] (Beimingwu) introduces a learnware dock system that generates specifications for pre-trained models, but it does not involve semantic graph-based labeling or ensemble reuse. Paper [13] (Nonlinear Multi-Model Reuse) discusses multi-model reuse but focuses on nonlinear reuse mechanisms rather than the specific MLL paradigm. None of the prior papers describe a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates MLL on a benchmark of 49 VLMs and 17 datasets, achieving state-of-the-art model-selection performance and demonstrating scalability with hub size. Paper [4] evaluates VLM selection methods but does not introduce a new benchmark or evaluation design. Paper [8] (LEMR) introduces MoraBench, a benchmark for label-efficient model ranking, but this is specific to NLP tasks and does not overlap with the introduced benchmark for VLMs. Paper [12] (VLUE) introduces a multi-task benchmark for evaluating VLMs, but it focuses on generalization ability rather than model selection. Paper [15] incorporates uncertainty quantification into VLM evaluation but does not overlap with the introduced benchmark design. The evaluation design appears to be novel.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of vision-language models (VLMs) for model selection and reuse. Paper [4] explicitly addresses VLM selection for downstream applications, and papers [12], [15], and [19] also work within the VLM domain. This domain is well-covered by prior work.

**PURPOSE**
The purpose is to enable efficient selection and reuse of models from a large pool without exhaustively evaluating each one on the target task. This is covered by multiple papers. For example, [4] states the goal is to address the fact that "exhaustive evaluation of all available VLMs on a novel application is not only time and computationally demanding". Similarly, [14] aims to "reduc[e] the search cost of the best pre-trained model over a large-scale model zoo for a downstream task."

**MECHANISM**
The mechanism involves a two-stage process: (1) an offline, task-independent characterization of each model to create a "label" or signature, and (2) a cheap online selection step that matches the target task to these pre-computed signatures. This primitive is covered by [24], which proposes an "offline phase [that] clusters the training data of each SE model to generate a representative vector for each model" and an "online phase [that] selects the best-matched model by calculating the distance between the test utterance and the representative vectors". This is the same design despite the domain difference (speech vs. vision).

**EVALUATION**
The evaluation design consists of applying the proposed selection method to a large pool of models and a suite of downstream tasks, then measuring the performance of the selected models against baselines. This design is not new. For instance, [4] uses the same design: "We evaluate our framework on a diverse set of 20 publicly available VLMs and 20 popular image classification datasets... Our method outperforms all baselines". The contribution introduces a new benchmark instance, but the evaluation design itself is covered.

**DOMAIN**
The domain is model selection and reuse for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). This is covered by several prior papers. For example, [4] is explicitly about "Language-Only Vision Model Selection", and [12] introduces "A Multi-Task Benchmark for Evaluating Vision-Language Models".

Paper [2] (IGLUE) aggregates datasets and creates new ones for benchmarking across modalities, tasks, and languages, which is substantively equivalent to constructing a benchmark for systematic evaluation. Paper [11] introduces baselines for model selection using a linearized framework, which also involves constructing a benchmark for evaluating pretrained models. Paper [22] proposes scalable methods for diverse model selection, which similarly involves benchmarking pretrained models across tasks.

The contribution evaluates 49 VLMs and 17 target datasets with per-task ground-truth rankings to validate effectiveness and scalability. Paper [11] uses a benchmark to validate model selection methods, which matches the evaluation design of benchmarking pretrained models for selection. Paper [22] also benchmarks pretrained models for transfer learning, validating their scalability and effectiveness. Both papers reuse the same evaluation design: benchmarking pretrained models across tasks with ground-truth rankings.

Paper [2] (IGLUE) explicitly addresses vision-and-language research, which is the same general application area. **PURPOSE: Provide a standardized way to evaluate VLM selection and reuse methods, which previously lacked benchmarks.**

Paper [11] introduces "a new benchmark for model selection for fine-tuning" explicitly addressing the lack of standardized evaluation for model selection methods. Paper [22] addresses "scalable diverse model selection" and benchmarks methods. Paper [17] studies "task adaptive pre-trained model selection" and evaluates methods. However, these focus on general vision/NLP models, not VLMs specifically. The purpose of providing a *standardized benchmark* for evaluating *model selection methods* is directly covered by [11], which states "we introduce two new baselines for model selection" and creates benchmark infrastructure for comparing model selection approaches. Paper [16] also jointly evaluates pretrained model selection methods across datasets.

**MECHANISM: Construction of a benchmark with 49 pre-trained VLMs and 17 target datasets, providing ground-truth model ranking per task, plus a semantic graph of >9000 visual concepts for labeling.**

The core primitives here are: (1) assembling a model zoo + dataset collection with ground-truth rankings, and (2) a semantic concept graph for labeling. Paper [11] constructs a benchmark with a model zoo and ground-truth rankings per task. Paper [22] builds a diverse model bank benchmark for transfer learning evaluation. The semantic graph of visual concepts is a distinct element — no prior paper describes constructing a semantic/ontological graph of visual concepts as part of a benchmark mechanism. Papers [7] mentions semantic zoom but is unrelated. No prior paper combines these two primitives (model zoo + semantic concept graph) in this way. The ground-truth ranking construction is covered by [11] and [22], but the semantic concept graph component appears absent.

**EVALUATION: Benchmark of 49 VLMs and 17 target datasets with per-task ground-truth rankings; used to validate effectiveness and scalability of MLL.**

The evaluation *design* — using a model zoo benchmark with multiple datasets and per-task ground-truth rankings to validate model selection methods — is used in [11] ("a linearized framework and a new benchmark for model selection"), [22] ("scalable diverse model selection" evaluated across model banks and datasets), and [16] (evaluating pretrained model selection across datasets). The design of "evaluate a model selection method against ground-truth rankings across many models and datasets" is clearly present in [11] and [22].

**DOMAIN: Vision-Language Models / benchmarking**

Paper [2] (IGLUE) explicitly works in vision-and-language benchmarking. Paper [1] and others touch on benchmarking. Paper [3] benchmarks vision transformers for transfer learning. The domain of VLM benchmarking is covered by [2], which is explicitly a "benchmark for transfer learning across modalities, tasks, and languages" in the vision-and-language space.
